title: II. He Gets Rid Of His Eldest Son
section: Book I — The History Of A Family
paragraphs: You can easily imagine what kind of father a man like that would make, and how he'd raise his children. His conduct as a father was exactly what you'd expect. He completely abandoned the child from his marriage to Adelaïda Ivanovna—not out of malice, and not because of some grudge over the marriage, but simply because he forgot about him. While he was wearing everyone out with his tears and complaints, and turning his house into a den of debauchery, a loyal family servant, Grigory, took the three-year-old Mitya under his wing. If he hadn't looked after him, there would have been no one even to change the baby's shirt.

It happened, too, that the child's relatives on his mother's side forgot about him at first as well. His grandfather was no longer living, his grandmother—Mitya's grandmother—had moved to Moscow and was seriously ill, and his aunts were all married, so Mitya spent almost a whole year in old Grigory's care, living with him in the servants' cottage. Even if his father had remembered him (and he couldn't have been entirely unaware of his existence), he would only have sent him back to the cottage, since the child would just have been in the way of his debaucheries. But a cousin of Mitya's mother, Pyotr Alexandrovitch Miüsov, happened to return from Paris around then. He would go on to live abroad for many years afterward, but at the time he was quite a young man, notable among the Miüsovs for his enlightened views and European polish, a man who had lived in the capitals and abroad. By the end of his life he had become a Liberal of the type common in the forties and fifties. Over the course of his career he'd come into contact with many of the most progressive men of his time, in Russia and abroad. He had known Proudhon and Bakunin personally, and in his later years loved to describe the three days of the Paris Revolution of February 1848, hinting that he himself had very nearly taken part in the fighting on the barricades. This was one of the most cherished memories of his youth. He had an independent fortune of about a thousand serfs, to use the old reckoning. His splendid estate lay on the outskirts of our little town and bordered the lands of our famous monastery, with which Pyotr Alexandrovitch, almost as soon as he came into the property, began an endless lawsuit—over fishing rights on the river, or timber rights in the forest, I don't know exactly which. He considered it his duty as a citizen and a man of culture to launch an attack on the “clericals.” Hearing all about Adelaïda Ivanovna, whom he of course remembered and had once been interested in, and learning that Mitya existed, he stepped in—despite all his youthful indignation and contempt for Fyodor Pavlovitch. He made the man's acquaintance for the first time, and told him directly that he wished to take charge of the child's education. He liked to tell, long afterward, as a telling detail, how when he first brought up Mitya, Fyodor Pavlovitch looked at him for a while as though he didn't understand which child was being discussed, and even seemed surprised to learn he had a little son living in the house. The story may have been exaggerated, but it must have been something close to the truth.

Fyodor Pavlovitch was fond, all his life, of playacting, of suddenly taking on some unexpected role, sometimes for no reason at all, even to his own direct disadvantage—as, for instance, in this very case. This habit, though, is characteristic of a good many people, including some quite clever ones, unlike Fyodor Pavlovitch. Pyotr Alexandrovitch pushed the matter through energetically, and was appointed, together with Fyodor Pavlovitch, joint guardian of the child, who had a small property—a house and some land—left to him by his mother. Mitya did indeed pass into this cousin's care, but since the cousin had no family of his own, and, having secured the income from his estate, was in a hurry to get back to Paris, he left the boy in the charge of one of his own cousins, a lady living in Moscow. As it turned out, once he'd settled permanently in Paris, he too forgot about the child, especially once the February Revolution broke out and made such an impression on him that he remembered it for the rest of his life. The Moscow lady died, and Mitya passed into the care of one of her married daughters. I believe he changed homes a fourth time after that. I won't go into it further now, since I'll have much more to say later about Fyodor Pavlovitch's firstborn, and for now I must confine myself to the most essential facts about him, without which I couldn't begin my story.

In the first place, this Mitya, or rather Dmitri Fyodorovitch, was the only one of Fyodor Pavlovitch's three sons who grew up believing he had property of his own, and that he'd be independent once he came of age. He spent an irregular boyhood and youth. He didn't finish his studies at the gymnasium; he got into a military school, then went to the Caucasus, was promoted, fought a duel, was busted down to the ranks, earned his rank back, lived wildly, and spent a good deal of money. He received no income at all from Fyodor Pavlovitch until he came of age, and until then ran up debts. He saw and met his father, Fyodor Pavlovitch, for the first time upon coming of age, when he visited our neighborhood specifically to settle accounts with him over the property. He doesn't seem to have liked his father. He didn't stay with him long, and hurried to get away, having only managed to obtain a sum of money and an agreement for future payments from the estate—the revenue and value of which he was unable, notably, to get any accounting of from his father on this occasion. Fyodor Pavlovitch noted for the first time then (this too is worth noting) that Mitya had a vague and inflated idea of his property. Fyodor Pavlovitch was quite pleased about this, since it suited his own designs perfectly. He gathered only that the young man was frivolous, unruly, violent-tempered, impatient, and dissipated, and that if he could just get hold of ready cash he'd be satisfied—for a short while, of course. So Fyodor Pavlovitch began exploiting this, sending him small doles and installments from time to time. In the end, four years later, when Mitya, out of patience, came a second time to our little town to settle things once and for all with his father, it turned out, to his astonishment, that he had nothing left—that it was hard even to get an accounting—that he had already received the full value of his property in sums of money from Fyodor Pavlovitch, and might even be in debt to him, that by various agreements he'd entered into of his own free will at various earlier dates, he had no right to expect anything more, and so on and so forth. The young man was overwhelmed, suspected fraud and cheating, and was nearly beside himself. And indeed, this circumstance led to the catastrophe that forms the subject of my first introductory story—or rather, its outward side. But before I get to that story, I must say a little about Fyodor Pavlovitch's other two sons, and where they came from.
